DMCA COUNTER-NOTIFICATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Hosting Inc.

COUNTER-NOTIFICATION DECLARATION
This counter notification is submitted to Acme Hosting Inc.'s designated agent under 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3) in response to the removal or disabling of material described below.

1. I am Jordan Alex Lee, the subscriber at whose direction the material identified below was posted or stored on Acme Hosting Inc.'s service.

2. The material that was removed or disabled, and the location at which it appeared on Acme Hosting Inc.'s service before it was removed or disabled, is identified as follows: a blog post titled 'Product Review', formerly located at https://example.com/blog/product-review.

3. I have a good faith belief that the material identified above was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled.

4. I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing statement is true and correct.

5. My contact information is: 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, (415) 555-0100.

6. I consent to the jurisdiction of the Federal District Court for the Northern District of California, and I will accept service of process from the person who provided the original takedown notification, or from that person's agent.

REQUIRED ELEMENTS OF AN EFFECTIVE COUNTER-NOTIFICATION
Federal copyright law specifies what a subscriber's counter notification must contain to be effective under 17 U.S.C. § 512(g) — the provision that lets a person whose material was removed in response to a takedown notification seek its restoration. To be effective, a counter notification must be a written communication, provided to the service provider's designated agent, that includes substantially four elements, in this order: first, a physical or electronic signature of the subscriber; second, identification of the material that has been removed or to which access has been disabled, and the location at which the material appeared before it was removed or disabled; third, a statement, made under penalty of perjury, that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled; and fourth, the subscriber's name, address, and telephone number, together with a statement that the subscriber consents to the jurisdiction of the federal district court for the judicial district where that address is located (or, if the address is outside the United States, any judicial district where the service provider may be found), and that the subscriber will accept service of process from the person who sent the original takedown notification or that person's agent. The statute places the signature requirement first and the sworn good-faith statement third, ahead of the contact-and-consent information, which comes last.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "To be effective under this subsection, a counter notification must be a written communication provided to the service provider’s designated agent that includes substantially the following: (A) A physical or electronic signature of the subscriber. (B) Identification of the material that has been removed or to which access has been disabled and the location at which the material appeared before it was removed or access to it was disabled. (C) A statement under penalty of perjury that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled. (D) The subscriber’s name, address, and telephone number, and a statement that the subscriber consents to the jurisdiction of Federal District Court for the judicial district in which the address is located, or if the subscriber’s address is outside of the United States, for any judicial district in which the service provider may be found, and that the subscriber will accept service of process from the person who provided notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) or an agent of such person."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, required contents of a counter notification (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of what 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3) requires a counter notification to contain — not a claim about whether any particular service provider's own counter-notification submission form asks for exactly this list and nothing more, or about how a specific platform processes a counter notification that is missing one of these elements. The companion DMCA Takedown Notice document in this corpus already quotes this same subsection, in the course of describing the put-back process generally, as part of a clause covering both the elements and the restoration timeline together; this clause is not an independent corroborating source from a different provision — it is the same statutory text, restated here as the primary subject of a document devoted to the counter-notification side of the process in more depth.

THE SWORN STATEMENT IS NARROW: MISTAKE OR MISIDENTIFICATION OF THE MATERIAL, NOT DISAGREEMENT OR FAIR USE
Federal copyright law limits what a counter notification's sworn statement may say. The statute requires a statement, made under penalty of perjury, that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled — a statement about whether the takedown targeted the wrong material, or was the product of some other error in identifying it, not a statement that the subscriber simply disagrees with the copyright owner's infringement claim on the merits. The provision does not ask the subscriber to swear that the use was authorized, that it qualifies as fair use, that the underlying copyright claim is invalid, or that the copyright owner is wrong about infringement generally — it asks only whether the takedown targeted the wrong material, or resulted from some other identification error. A subscriber whose actual objection is that their use was fair use, or that the copyright owner has no valid claim, is being asked by this specific sworn statement to address something narrower than either of those positions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A statement under penalty of perjury that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, the required good-faith statement's specific ground (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the specific, narrow content 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3)(C) requires the counter notification's sworn statement to have — not legal advice about whether a particular removal was, in fact, a mistake or misidentification, whether a particular subscriber's belief is held in good faith, or how a court would treat a counter notification framed around a fair-use or non-infringement argument instead of the statutory mistake-or-misidentification language, which is a question of statutory interpretation this clause does not resolve. This is the same subsection quoted in the companion DMCA Takedown Notice document's dmca_counternotice_putback clause in this corpus, as part of that document's summary of the full counter-notification-elements list; this clause is not an independent corroborating source from elsewhere — it restates the same statutory text to focus specifically on interpreting what the sworn statement is, and is not, permitted to say.

ONLY THE SUBSCRIBER MAY FILE A COUNTER-NOTIFICATION, AND DOING SO FORWARDS THE SUBSCRIBER'S REAL IDENTITY
Federal copyright law's counter-notification mechanism belongs to the 'subscriber' — the statute's term for the person at whose direction the removed material resided on the service provider's system or network before it was taken down. Section 512 does not separately define 'subscriber' anywhere, including in the subsection that defines other terms used throughout the section (which defines only 'service provider' and 'monetary relief'); the word is used in its ordinary sense, referring to the person whose account or posting held the material. Filing an effective counter notification requires disclosing that subscriber's real name, address, and telephone number, together with a statement consenting to the jurisdiction of the applicable federal district court and agreeing to accept service of process — and the statute requires the service provider, on receiving a valid counter notification, to promptly provide a copy of it (which necessarily includes that identifying and jurisdictional information) to the person who sent the original takedown notification. An anonymous or pseudonymous poster who wants the counter-notification process to work as the statute describes faces a practical consequence built into this design: using it means the poster's real identity and address reach the party who complained about the material, as a direct result of the forwarding step the statute itself requires.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "material residing at the direction of a subscriber of the service provider on a system or network controlled or operated by or for the service provider"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, the subscriber whose material was removed (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  "The subscriber’s name, address, and telephone number, and a statement that the subscriber consents to the jurisdiction of Federal District Court for the judicial district in which the address is located, or if the subscriber’s address is outside of the United States, for any judicial district in which the service provider may be found, and that the subscriber will accept service of process from the person who provided notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) or an agent of such person."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3)(D) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, subscriber's real name, address, and telephone number required (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  "upon receipt of a counter notification described in paragraph (3), promptly provides the person who provided the notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) with a copy of the counter notification, and informs that person that it will replace the removed material or cease disabling access to it in 10 business days; and"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, service provider must forward the counter notification to the complaining party (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  "(k) Definitions.— (1) Service provider.— (A) As used in subsection (a), the term “service provider” means an entity offering the transmission, routing, or providing of connections for digital online communications, between or among points specified by a user, of material of the user’s choosing, without modification to the content of the material as sent or received. (B) As used in this section, other than subsection (a), the term “service provider” means a provider of online services or network access, or the operator of facilities therefor, and includes an entity described in subparagraph (A). (2) Monetary relief.— As used in this section, the term “monetary relief” means damages, costs, attorneys’ fees, and any other form of monetary payment."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(k) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definitions used in section 512 — 'subscriber' is not among them (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that 17 U.S.C. § 512 uses the term 'subscriber' without separately defining it, that an effective counter notification must include the subscriber's real name, address, and telephone number under § 512(g)(3)(D), and that § 512(g)(2)(B) requires the service provider to forward the counter notification to the original complaining party — not a claim about how any particular service provider actually handles or redacts that forwarded information in practice, about whether a specific platform allows a counter notification to be filed with real contact information withheld from public view while still being forwarded privately to the complaining party (the statutory forwarding obligation runs to that party regardless of what is or isn't made public), or about safety, immigration, or other consequences that might follow from a particular person's identity being disclosed to a particular complaining party. All citations below are to subsections of the single statutory section 17 U.S.C. § 512 (subsections (g) and (k)), fetched from the same primary-source page; they are listed separately for precision but are treated as one source, not independent, corroborating sources.

THE PUT-BACK SEQUENCE: NOTICE TO THE SUBSCRIBER, FORWARDING, AND THE 10-TO-14-BUSINESS-DAY RESTORATION WINDOW
Federal copyright law ties a service provider's protection from liability to the subscriber — for taking down material in the first place — to the provider following a specific three-step sequence once it removes or disables material in response to a takedown notification. First, the provider must take reasonable steps promptly to notify the subscriber that it has removed or disabled access to the material. Second, if the subscriber then submits a valid counter notification, the provider must promptly provide a copy of it to the person who sent the original takedown notification, and inform that person that the provider will restore the material in 10 business days. Third, the provider must actually restore the material — replacing it or ceasing to disable access to it — not less than 10, nor more than 14, business days after receiving the counter notification, unless its designated agent first receives notice that the person who sent the original notification has filed an action seeking a court order to restrain the subscriber from the allegedly infringing activity. That exception is narrow: it requires the complaining party to have actually filed a lawsuit seeking that specific kind of court order, not merely to have objected, sent a follow-up letter, or threatened legal action. The statute measures the window in business days, not calendar days, and does not itself define what counts as a business day.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "unless the service provider— (A) takes reasonable steps promptly to notify the subscriber that it has removed or disabled access to the material;"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, prompt notice to the subscriber of the removal (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  "upon receipt of a counter notification described in paragraph (3), promptly provides the person who provided the notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) with a copy of the counter notification, and informs that person that it will replace the removed material or cease disabling access to it in 10 business days; and (C) replaces the removed material and ceases disabling access to it not less than 10, nor more than 14, business days following receipt of the counter notice, unless its designated agent first receives notice from the person who submitted the notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) that such person has filed an action seeking a court order to restrain the subscriber from engaging in infringing activity relating to the material on the service provider’s system or network."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2)(B)-(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, forwarding the counter notification and the restoration window (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the sequence and timing 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2) sets for restoring removed material — not a claim about whether any particular service provider actually follows this sequence in a given case, about how a specific platform's internal restoration process works, or about what counts as a 'business day' for a particular provider, which the statute does not define. Compliance with this sequence is what preserves the provider's own liability protection under this subsection (addressed in a companion clause in this document), not a duty a subscriber can necessarily compel a court to enforce on its own; this clause does not claim otherwise. Both citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2); they are treated as one source, not independent, corroborating sources. The companion DMCA Takedown Notice document in this corpus already quotes § 512(g)(2)(B)-(C); this clause adds the preceding step, § 512(g)(2)(A), which a document focused on sending a takedown notice does not need to dwell on.

MISREPRESENTATION LIABILITY APPLIES TO A FALSE COUNTER-NOTIFICATION, NOT JUST A FALSE TAKEDOWN NOTICE
Federal copyright law's misrepresentation-liability provision applies in both directions. A person who knowingly materially misrepresents, in a submission made under the notice-and-takedown provisions, either that material or activity is infringing (the takedown-notice direction) or that material or activity was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification (the counter-notification direction) is liable for any damages — including costs and attorney's fees — incurred by whoever is injured by the misrepresentation, as a result of the service provider relying on it. For a false counter notification specifically, the person typically exposed to this liability is the subscriber who submitted it, and the party typically injured is the copyright owner or its authorized licensee whose material was restored, or ceased being disabled, based on the subscriber's sworn but knowingly false statement that removal was a mistake or misidentification. The statute lists the same set of potentially injured parties — the alleged infringer, a copyright owner or its authorized licensee, or a service provider — for either direction of misrepresentation, because whichever way the misrepresentation runs, any of those parties could end up being the one harmed by the service provider's reliance on it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person who knowingly materially misrepresents under this section— (1) that material or activity is infringing, or (2) that material or activity was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification, shall be liable for any damages, including costs and attorneys’ fees, incurred by the alleged infringer, by any copyright owner or copyright owner’s authorized licensee, or by a service provider, who is injured by such misrepresentation, as the result of the service provider relying upon such misrepresentation in removing or disabling access to the material or activity claimed to be infringing, or in replacing the removed material or ceasing to disable access to it."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(f) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, misrepresentations in a takedown notice or counter-notification (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that 17 U.S.C. § 512(f) creates a damages remedy for a knowing material misrepresentation made in either a takedown notice or a counter notification — not a claim about whether any particular counter notification meets that standard, which turns on facts (including the subscriber's actual, subjective state of mind in swearing to a mistake-or-misidentification belief, not merely whether the subscriber turned out to be wrong) that this clause doesn't resolve. This is the same statutory subsection already quoted in the companion DMCA Takedown Notice document's dmca_misrepresentation_liability clause in this corpus, which addresses both directions in a single sentence; this clause restates the same text to focus specifically on the counter-notification direction, which that document treats only briefly. A well-known Ninth Circuit decision, Lenz v. Universal Music Corp., addressed what 'knowingly materially misrepresents' means under this subsection (in the takedown-notice direction); it could not be independently verified for this clause because the CourtListener research tool returned a daily rate-limit error (125 requests/day, next available in roughly 10 hours) on the attempt made while researching this document, so it is omitted from the citations below rather than quoted from memory. This topic is primarily statutory, and case law is not required to support the clause.

WHY A SERVICE PROVIDER HAS AN INCENTIVE TO FOLLOW THIS PROCESS: ITS OWN SAFE HARBOR DEPENDS ON IT
Federal copyright law gives a service provider its own reason, independent of any duty it owes to a particular subscriber, to follow the counter-notification and put-back procedure correctly. As a general matter, a service provider is not liable to any person for a claim based on its good-faith removal of material believed to be infringing, regardless of whether the material turns out to be infringing. But that protection does not apply to a claim by the subscriber whose material was removed unless the service provider also does three things: promptly notifies the subscriber of the removal, promptly forwards a valid counter notification to the original complaining party while telling that party it will restore the material in 10 business days, and then actually restores the material within the 10-to-14-business-day window described elsewhere in this document (or continues withholding it, without losing this protection, if the complaining party has filed suit seeking a restraining court order in that window). A service provider that skips or botches these steps loses this particular liability shield with respect to the subscriber whose material it removed — which is a reason built into the statute's own incentive structure for a service provider to follow the process, not a promise this document makes about what any specific platform will actually do in a given case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Subject to paragraph (2), a service provider shall not be liable to any person for any claim based on the service provider’s good faith disabling of access to, or removal of, material or activity claimed to be infringing or based on facts or circumstances from which infringing activity is apparent, regardless of whether the material or activity is ultimately determined to be infringing. (2) Exception.—Paragraph (1) shall not apply with respect to material residing at the direction of a subscriber of the service provider on a system or network controlled or operated by or for the service provider that is removed, or to which access is disabled by the service provider, pursuant to a notice provided under subsection (c)(1)(C), unless the service provider—"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(1)-(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, the liability shield and its conditions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  "A service provider’s compliance with paragraph (2) shall not subject the service provider to liability for copyright infringement with respect to the material identified in the notice provided under subsection (c)(1)(C)."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, limitation on other liability for compliant restoration (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/512)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the incentive structure 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(1)-(2) creates for a service provider — not a claim about whether any particular service provider follows this process correctly, promptly, or at all in a given case, or about what remedy (if any) a subscriber has against a provider that does not. The protection described in this clause is a liability shield running to the service provider, not an independent legal duty a court will necessarily order the provider to perform on a subscriber's demand. This clause also quotes § 512(g)(4), which describes a related but separate protection — a service provider's compliance with the paragraph (2) sequence does not expose it to copyright-infringement liability toward the original complaining party for restoring the material. Both citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, 17 U.S.C. § 512(g); they are treated as one source, not independent, corroborating sources.

Jordan Alex Lee
Date: October 15, 2026

That exception is narrow: it requires the complaining party to have actually filed a lawsuit seeking that specific kind of court order, not merely to have objected, sent a follow-up letter, or threatened legal action. The statute measures the window in business days, not calendar days, and does not itself define what counts as a business day.

expectedJSON.body: Federal copyright law's misrepresentation-liability provision applies in both directions. A person who knowingly materially misrepresents, in a submission made under the notice-and-takedown provisions, either that material or activity is infringing (the takedown-notice direction) or that material or activity was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification (the counter-notification direction) is liable for any damages — including costs and attorney's fees — incurred by whoever is injured by the misrepresentation, as a result of the service provider relying on it. For a false counter notification specifically, the person typically exposed to this liability is the subscriber who submitted it, and the party typically injured is the copyright owner or its authorized licensee whose material was restored, or ceased being disabled, based on the subscriber's sworn but knowingly false statement that removal was a mistake or misidentification. The statute lists the same set of potentially injured parties — the alleged infringer, a copyright owner or its authorized licensee, or a service provider — for either direction of misrepresentation, because whichever way the misrepresentation runs, any of those parties could end up being the one harmed by the service provider's reliance on it.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, misrepresentations in a takedown notice or counter-notification
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly materially misrepresents under this section— (1) that material or activity is infringing, or (2) that material or activity was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification, shall be liable for any damages, including costs and attorneys’ fees, incurred by the alleged infringer, by any copyright owner or copyright owner’s authorized licensee, or by a service provider, who is injured by such misrepresentation, as the result of the service provider relying upon such misrepresentation in removing or disabling access to the material or activity claimed to be infringing, or in replacing the removed material or ceasing to disable access to it.

expectedJSON.body: Federal copyright law gives a service provider its own reason, independent of any duty it owes to a particular subscriber, to follow the counter-notification and put-back procedure correctly. As a general matter, a service provider is not liable to any person for a claim based on its good-faith removal of material believed to be infringing, regardless of whether the material turns out to be infringing. But that protection does not apply to a claim by the subscriber whose material was removed unless the service provider also does three things: promptly notifies the subscriber of the removal, promptly forwards a valid counter notification to the original complaining party while telling that party it will restore the material in 10 business days, and then actually restores the material within the 10-to-14-business-day window described elsewhere in this document (or continues withholding it, without losing this protection, if the complaining party has filed suit seeking a restraining court order in that window). A service provider that skips or botches these steps loses this particular liability shield with respect to the subscriber whose material it removed — which is a reason built into the statute's own incentive structure for a service provider to follow the process, not a promise this document makes about what any specific platform will actually do in a given case.

(2) Exception.—Paragraph (1) shall not apply with respect to material residing at the direction of a subscriber of the service provider on a system or network controlled or operated by or for the service provider that is removed, or to which access is disabled by the service provider, pursuant to a notice provided under subsection (c)(1)(C), unless the service provider—

citations.quote: A service provider’s compliance with paragraph (2) shall not subject the service provider to liability for copyright infringement with respect to the material identified in the notice provided under subsection (c)(1)(C).
